The shouting match found the real grievance — the 14,783-gold ledger — and the negotiation found the real exit: a 60/30 split on publication. The radio then supplied the next problem: Star Hill Clinic is reportedly locked down, with Luigi inside.

sections.name: I. The Revision on the Balcony
sections.overview:
Two weeks of quiet is a long time in this archive, and I had spent all fourteen days of it the same way: on the balcony, at the patio table, with the night sky open above me and Wario's residence sitting on its peak like a paperweight on the horizon. You cannot renovate away a sightline. I have asked.

The draft in my hands was 'No Longer Brothers — Revision 2, Working Title', and a working title is a confession that the work is not done. I read it aloud, because a draft read silently lies to its author. The cold took each line as I gave it: *"He didn't just walk away; he walked into a void where our shared history was erased by his own choice."* A good sentence. Too good — the kind that sounds true because it is well dressed — and I crossed out two of its neighbours for keeping bad company. The ink bled where the pen dug in. My verdict, spoken to nobody: *"This won't work. It needs to be more refined for publishing."*

I read the last line anyway, the one underlined so hard the nib had nearly torn the wood-pulp: *"If he is no longer my brother, then I am finally free from his shadow."* The words went out over the stone railing and did not come back. Somewhere below a dog barked twice, sharp enough to make the page tremble in my grip — or the page trembled on its own; the record permits both readings. Then a gust crossed the patio and took the candle, and I sat in the dark with the smell of spent wick and damp stone and distant woodsmoke, the title of my own paper going cold in my hands. Up on the peak, though I did not know it yet, somebody had been watching my light burn.
sections.waluigi_note: Editing aloud is a professional practice, not a performance. Everything after this section happened because a man with a telescope and a ledger decided otherwise. I stand by the method, and I am invoicing him for the candle.

sections.name: II. The Light Leaves the Mountain
sections.overview:
I was packing up when the mountain moved. Papers into the satchel, the grimoire a familiar weight against my side, boots clicking on stone that had already gone cold for the night — and then light, where no light belongs at that hour. A flare from the upper windows of Wario's residence, hard and white, cutting down the slope like somebody had opened a furnace door. I stood still and watched a speck detach itself from the house and start down the mountainside, deliberate as a finger moving down a column of figures.

Then the speck stopped being a speck. The sound arrived first, the way bad news does: a low thrum through the stones of the balcony, into the patio table, into my teeth. The shape lifted off the peak and resolved into rotors and a searchlight, and the searchlight was not sweeping the valley. It was coming here.

*"What in the world is he doing with a chopper?!"* I said it aloud to the same cold air that had taken my draft, and the air declined to answer. The downdraft arrived ahead of the machine itself, flattening my coat against my back, snapping the loose corner of every paper I had not yet bagged. I counted my options the way you count teeth after a fall: the door behind me, the satchel on my shoulder, the distance between the two.

The helicopter did not hover politely at the property line. It came in low over the patio, belly nearly skimming the railing, and the first words of the negotiation — because that is what this evening was, though neither of us had said so yet — came down through a loudhailer, distorted by turbine whine and the particular acoustics of a man who has never once modulated his volume indoors or out: *"GET OUT HERE!"*
sections.waluigi_note: Fourteen days of silence and his opening position was a searchlight. Note the order of events for the ledger: he watched my candle first, and billed me second. The surveillance was free. It is the only thing he has ever given me at no charge.

sections.name: III. "YOU'RE HIDING AGAIN"
sections.overview:
The searchlight found me before I found the door. It pinned me against the stone wall the way a collector pins a moth — white glare, two dimensions, nowhere to file a complaint. I ran for the balcony door with the satchel banging my hip and the draft clutched in one fist, boots skidding on tile the frost had already licked, and the helicopter swept low enough on its pass that I felt the belly of the machine go over me like a hand checking a shelf for dust.

*"YOU'RE HIDING AGAIN!"* The loudhailer cracked on the word 'hiding' — there was something in the voice beyond the usual volume, a fray at the edges I would have called panic in a man who permitted himself any.

*"WAH! Hiding?! No — I am researching! Yeah, researching!"* I gave him the truth at the top of my lungs, which is the one register in which the truth sounds exactly like a lie. *"Luigi is still in the hospital, so—"*

He did not let the sentence land. *"RESEARCHING? YOU'VE BEEN RESEARCHING FOR WEEKS!"* And then, through the rotor wash and the rattling windowpanes, the line that mattered more than every decibel around it: *"THE DOCTOR SAYS HE CAN'T MOVE YET! WE NEED TO MOVE!"*

I want the record to hold that line the way I held it, mid-stumble, over the threshold: the doctor says. Present tense. Somebody had been checking on the patient — recently, personally, or through somebody paid to be personal. It was not me. I had spent two weeks interrogating a draft about the brothers while the only brother still reachable lay in a clinic bed, and the man I file under 'allied capitalist hazard' had fresher information about him than the archive did.
sections.waluigi_note: He shouted a timekeeping dispute at me — weeks, I said two days later it had been two days, and we were both wrong by the calendar. But 'the doctor says he can't move yet' was current intelligence. File the evening's first wound here: the greedy man was better informed about the hurt one than I was.

sections.name: IV. The Claw with the W
sections.overview:
The helicopter's underbelly opened and delivered the evening's thesis. A mechanical claw on a reinforced arm — yellow and black, scaled like a drawbridge winch, and painted on its housing, in case posterity should wonder whose fist was coming through a scholar's door at midnight, a single enormous 'W'. The man monogrammes his siege equipment. I noted it even while running, because that is the job.

It swung out like a grappling hook and came down on the balcony stones close enough that the shock of it travelled up through my boot heels. Talons the size of fireplace pokers scraped across the patio, gathering a screech of granite, and I lunged for the entrance with my lungs full of rotor wash and grit. *"Weeks? No, no — it's been two days, right?"* I shouted it mid-stride, a man litigating the calendar while the calendar tried to kill him. The answer came back frayed and furious: *"TWO DAYS? YOU'RE LOSING YOUR MIND!"*

The claw snapped forward as I reached the handle. It hit the frame beside my head — the impact went through the door, through the wall, through the building's bones and into mine — and for one breath the metal talons and my fingers shared the same square foot of architecture. I threw my weight forward. The door slammed with a sound like a book closing on a century, and the engine roar cut to a ringing, pressurized silence.

I stood in my own hallway, back against the oak, holding a crossed-out draft and approximately none of my composure. On the other side of two inches of wood: a fist the size of a wardrobe, and a creditor.
sections.waluigi_note: Respect for the door, which held the first exchange and is the only party to this evening that performed beyond its specification. It will be remembered. It will also, knowing my counterparty, be invoiced to me somehow.

sections.name: V. Four Strikes on Oak
sections.overview:
The silence lasted as long as it took him to convert the claw from a hand into an argument. Then the first strike came, and the heavy oak groaned the way old wood groans when it understands the situation before you do. I retreated through the hallway into the main study — my study, the good room, the one with the shelves that go up into the dark and the drafting tables cluttered with half-finished maps and scrolls whose provenance I would rather not shout through a door.

The air in there is always thick with old parchment and dry wax. That night it also carried frost off my own coat and the metallic taste the rotor wash had left on my tongue. The second strike put a splintering crack through the room like a rifle report. The third punched a chunk out of the frame, and through the gap came lamplight-coloured chaos: wind, grit, and my research answering the draft — loose sheets of 'The Tape' lifting off the drafting table and drifting toward the breach as if volunteering for evidence.

*"OPEN THE DOOR!"* The voice came through the wood muffled but undiminished, rattling the glass in the lanterns.

I was cornered between a bookshelf and the heavy mahogany table, running the arithmetic a man runs when the machine is bigger than he is: I could not beat the fist. Every second I spent deciding, it spent crushing the frame that stood between it and months of compiled work. A smaller claw — pincers, delicate, horrible — poked through a crack higher up and snapped at the air, tasting the room.
sections.waluigi_note: The fist was never going to take the research. It was going to destroy it incidentally, which is worse, because there is nobody to negotiate with inside the word 'incidentally'. That distinction is why everything in the next section happened.

sections.name: VI. Ice Storm in My Own Study
sections.overview:
I dove behind the mahogany table and made the only choice a scholar gets when the room is the hostage: freeze the library to save it. *"Ice Storm,"* I said — you say the words sharply or you say them twice — and pushed the mana through the syllables with a desperation I will edit out of every future retelling. The temperature in the study dropped like a verdict. Frost erupted from behind the table in a jagged crystalline wave, rolled over the carpets, and slammed into the door and the breaching fist together.

The physics did their work gratis: freezing moisture expanding inside split oak, cracking with loud pops, rime sheeting over yellow-and-black steel, slicking the talons until the arm lurched and lost its purchase on the frame. Ten points of mana, and worth every one. The gears behind the claw ground and complained; the fist jerked in its jagged white cage.

My own breath came out as weather. Everything on the drafting tables wore a skin of frost — maps, scrolls, the drifting pages of 'The Tape' now pinned mid-flight like insects in amber. I had bought a pause, not a victory, and the pause was already cracking at its edges.
sections.waluigi_note: Yes: I defended the papers about the brothers who burned by freezing the room. Somewhere a poet is insufferable about this, and I will not be providing their name to the archive.

sections.name: VII. The Shelf Pays Rent
sections.overview:
A library earns its keep exactly once. With the fist grinding against my first frost and the pause shrinking, I went to the nearest shelf and pulled titles the way a drowning man pulls at water — *"there has to be something in here that will help"* — and the shelf, for the first time in its pampered existence, helped.

A leather-bound treatise with a frost-touched seal: 'Atmospheric Displacement', a specialist text on keeping high-energy environments contained. I did not read it; there is no reading at that tempo. I flipped it open across the drafting table and let my fingers run the pages for a technique with the right shape, and found one with a name even a panicking man could operate: Flash-Freeze. Take any gas or moisture and solidify it. A wall, in other words. A wall made of exactly what the room was already full of.

Behind me the door gave another shudder, and wood shards skipped across the desk like thrown teeth. The smaller pincer-claw was working the upper crack wider, patient as interest. I put my palm flat on the open page, took the shape of the technique into my head sideways — borrowed, not learned; the distinction matters to wizards and to nobody else at midnight — and turned back toward the breach with the last of my mana gathering cold behind my teeth.
sections.waluigi_note: Months from now some scholar will ask whether I had a licence for an unstudied displacement technique. The answer is that the licencing office was unavailable, on account of a fist. The book goes back on the shelf with a commendation.

sections.name: VIII. The Wall
sections.overview:
*"Flash-Freeze!"* I poured everything left into it — the sting of the cold coming back up my own arms was the receipt — and the frost on the door stopped being weather and became architecture.

It petrified. The sheet of rime thickened into a jagged, glassy wall, flowing up into the splintered frame, sealing the shards of the ruined door in place like flaws in crystal. The expansion caught the mechanical fist mid-advance and closed on it with the sound of a vise closing on bone — a metal groan rising into a high screech of gears as the machine behind the wood discovered what every creditor eventually discovers: the asset can refuse.

For a moment, the first true moment since the light left the mountain, the thudding stopped. The study stood blue-white and silent: frost webbed across the shelves, my breath hanging in sheets, the trapped claw ticking as its joints cooled, and somewhere beyond the ice the steady beat of rotors, patient, like a man drumming fingers on a desk the size of the sky.

Through two inches of oak and a hand's-width of ice, the siege finally introduced itself honestly. But that belongs to the next section; this one ends with the wall, because the wall is the only thing I built all evening that did exactly what I asked.
sections.waluigi_note: The ledger of the defence, for auditors: one Ice Storm, one borrowed Flash-Freeze, forty points of mana spent in total, zero pages lost. Put it next to his fuel bill and his monogrammed grapple and tell me again which of us is bad with money.

sections.name: IX. It Was Never About the Brothers
sections.overview:
We argued through the ice, and the argument shed its costumes one at a time, in descending order of dignity.

*"WARIO! You're-a coocoo crazy! My house — you-a DESTROYED it! WAH!"* — a reasonable opening from the owner of the house.

*"YOUR HOUSE? I'M SAVING THE RECORDS!"* Costume one: rescuer. It held for a sentence. *"THEY'RE THE ONLY PROOF!"* Costume two: archivist-by-force, a man who had decided my narrative was evidence and evidence was his. There was desperation under it that I had not heard from him before, a crack in the boom. And when I pressed — *"wait, this isn't about before, is it?"* — the last costume came off with its coat: *"IT'S ABOUT THE DEBT!"*

There it was. Fourteen thousand, seven hundred and eighty-three gold pieces, delivered through a frozen door at full volume, matching the figure in his own file to the coin. *"The-a... partnership expenses? You-a still remember that — I thought you-a paused it! WAH! I haven't authorized 15% monthly interest on anything, you LIE!"* His answer ignored the interest entirely and went to scripture: *"THE CONTRACT IS BINDING, WALUIGI!"* A shard of my wall cracked loose and fell at the sheer volume of it.

And then the sentence that reclassified the whole evening, screamed by a man who by his own account had not slept in days: *"EVERYONE IS DISTRACTED BY THE LOST BROTHER, BUT I AM THE ONLY ONE LOOKING AT THE NUMBERS!"* The record files his delivery as unhinged and his bookkeeping as immaculate, and notes with some discomfort that both can be true at once.
sections.waluigi_note: I dispute the principal, the interest, and the hour of collection, in that order, in writing, forever. But the figure had not drifted a single coin in all these years. The most trustworthy thing about the man is the most alarming thing about him.

sections.name: X. The Pouch and the Word 'Settlement'
sections.overview:
De-escalation came in two currencies, and the first was the old-fashioned kind.

*"Alright, alright — I'll pay-a you some money, just please, no more destroying my house."* The change in him was audible through ice and oak together: *"GOLD! I WANT THE GOLD!"* — the frantic edge gone for exactly one half-second, replaced by a booming, almost childlike glee, and beneath the rotor noise I could hear, unmistakably, the rhythmic thud of a large man dancing.

I went into my tunic for the worn leather pouch I keep for personal expenditures and tipped it out on the study
 floor — heavy coins ringing on cold stone, roughly a hundred and fifty gold once the rolling ones were chased down. *"There. Are you-a happy?"*

*"THAT'S A START, WALUIGI!"* He did not count it. That is the detail the record wants kept: the man who knows his principal to the coin did not count the coins. The mechanical fist had gone still at the word 'settlement' the way a struck bell goes quiet — it was never about this amount, or honestly about any amount reachable by pouch. It was about the ledger seeing movement. The fist idled. The dancing stopped. Somewhere above, the searchlight drifted off my window for the first time in an hour, and the negotiation proper could finally begin.
sections.waluigi_note: A hundred and fifty gold against fourteen thousand is not a payment, it is a pulse — proof of life from the debt. He priced it accordingly and so did I. The real instrument was always going to be made of paper, not metal.

sections.name: XI. The Sixty-Thirty Split
sections.overview:
Then I made the offer that ended the siege, shouted through my own ice wall with the last of my breath and most of my pride.

*"Listen — how about this. Once we get Luigi back, we use his-a testimony — I publish the 'No Longer Brothers' narrative, and we split-a the profits. I'll give you the bigger— the sixty-thirty split, WAH! Just stop destroying my house!"*

*"A SIXTY-THIRTY SPLIT?!"* His voice went up past the turbine's register. And then — silence. The longest of the night. Through the wall I could hear him breathing, heavy and deliberate, the sound of a man running numbers in the dark. The ice ticked. The rotors beat. My heart audited itself.

The grinding gear-sound that followed was the arm withdrawing — fully, cleanly, out of my wall and off my property line. *"THEN YOU BETTER START WRITING THE CONTRACT BEFORE I CHANGE MY MIND!"*

I wrote it at the drafting table in under a minute, in a hand I will deny under oath, and passed it out through the breach. The great claw took the page with a delicacy that frightened me more than the four strikes had — pincers like a surgeon who moonlights as a pickpocket. A low chuckle came through clearly for the first time all evening, with the turbine suddenly under it instead of over it. *"A PROPER DEAL,"* he growled, frantic rage gone, cold satisfaction in its chair. *"I'LL HOLD THE CONTRACT AS COLLATERAL UNTIL THE FIRST PAYMENT IS SETTLED."*

The hand retracted into the dark. I stood in the ringing quiet of my ruined doorway and breathed like a man who had just co-signed something with the weather.
sections.waluigi_note: I have made the ledger my co-author. He is now financially upstream of my publication schedule, which is the most dangerous editing decision of my career and — I will say it once, quietly, here — probably the correct one.

sections.name: XII. The Golden Cage Report
sections.overview:
I walked out onto my own balcony like a visitor, through grit and shattered rime, and looked up at him.

Wario stood at the platform's edge with the searchlights behind him, silhouetted like a statue commissioned by itself, grinning the grin of a man holding collateral. *"YOU'VE GOT A GOOD HEAD ON YOUR SHOULDERS, WALUIGI,"* he bellowed, eyes gleaming like the coins still on my study floor. *"NOW WE JUST HAVE TO FIND THAT GREEN IDIOT BEFORE THE DEBT COLLECTORS GET BORED!"*

*"Luigi is still with Doctor Toad,"* I said, boarding the platform — quietly, but boarding. *"I haven't checked on him since that night. You have informants. Is he still there?"* Wario grabbed the radio and barked: *"REPORT! STATUS OF THE STAR HILL CLINIC, IMMEDIATELY!"* Static. Then a frantic voice confirming that Dr. Toad's facility is under heavy lockdown, for 'medical complications'.

*"Wah? They're-a locking the injured man up?"*

*"THEY CALL IT 'PROTECTION'. I CALL IT A CONVENIENT EXCUSE FOR DELAYING MY PAYMENT!"* He gripped my shoulder with a hand like a dock clamp, eyes wide, voice dropping into the register he saves for money in danger: *"IF HE'S STILL IN THAT CLINIC, EVERY SECOND WE WAIT IS A SECOND THEY GET TO HIDE HIS ASSETS!"*

The helicopter banked off my ruined balcony toward Star Hill with both signatories of the Contract of Accord aboard. Below us my outpost shrank to a lit doorway with no door in it. Ahead, a clinic that had stopped answering, two weeks into a two-week rest order, with the only reachable brother inside.
sections.waluigi_note: The lockdown claim has exactly one source: an informant paid by the man who profits from urgency, relayed at volume by that same man. I boarded anyway. File both halves of that sentence — the scepticism and the boots — because the archive should remember I carried both aboard.

aftermath: The outpost stands, minus a door and plus a frost scar. The Contract of Accord travels in Wario's keeping — the first paper he has ever held that pays him more if Waluigi publishes, which aligns the two of them more honestly than any apology could. The 150 gold is logged against a principal neither party agrees on. The next move was chosen by a radio: Star Hill Clinic, the lockdown report, and whatever 'medical complications' turns out to mean when the people saying it know they are being recorded. What 'medical complications' turned out to mean is filed in the sequel: the helicopter never reached the clinic door, and the man in Luigi's clothes was standing in the street outside it. See *The Rot-Zone at Star Hill*.

reputationNotes.waluigi: Paid on the spot under siege, then converted a hostile collection action into a signed revenue-sharing accord — the Enterprise respects nothing more than a counterparty who closes.
reputationNotes.wario: The Enterprise books a signed contract and a first payment; the Regency books a helicopter assault on a private residence over an invoice. Both entries are accurate.

waluigiAssessment:
1. The siege read as a rescue of records for exactly two sentences, and as a collection action for the rest of its life. File the first reading as what Wario needed to believe and the second as what the machinery was built for.
2. The 14,783-gold figure arrived through a frozen door matching the ledger in Wario's own file to the coin. Whatever else the man has lost — sleep, proportion, a door that was not his — the numbers have not drifted. That consistency is the most trustworthy thing about him and the most alarming.
3. The Star Hill lockdown is radio chatter from a paid informant, relayed by a creditor who profits from urgency. It enters the investigation as a lead with a named source, not as a fact. If it proves true, the question is not 'is Luigi safe' but 'who decided he should be unreachable, and on which day of the rest order.'
4. The sixty-thirty split is the real event here. Every prior paper between these two recorded what one of them owed the other. This is the first that pays them both for the same outcome. Watch what that does to the siege equipment.

name: The Rot-Zone at Star Hill
title: The Rot-Zone at Star Hill: A Fired Pilot, a Roof That Was Not a Landing Pad, the Man With Too Many Hands, and the Notebook That Left in a Courier's Satchel
date: 2 Aethel, 1035 BF — night, continuing without a break from the Debt Siege; the helicopter leg from the outpost to Star Hill
timeWindow: 2 Aethel, 1035 BF — one night: the helicopter leg from Waluigi's Outpost, the crash on the storehouse roof beside Dr. Toad's clinic, the stairwell, the street, and the loss of the notebook; Waluigi unconscious for 'three heartbeats of the market'
era: The Mushroom Kingdom Regency Era (1030s BF) — Mario's Disappearance Arc
type: Session Event / Crash and Retreat / Arc Escalation
location: Star Hill — the airspace over the valley, the flat roof of the storehouse beside Dr. Toad's Star Hill Clinic, its stairwell, and the clinic's main street
status: Unresolved — the clinic was not reached; Luigi's presence in the 'private wing' is unverified; Waluigi's working notebook is in the possession of a courier named Paulo; Mr. L sighted outside the clinic in at least three copies; the fired pilot's fate is unrecorded
summary: Straight off the Debt Siege, Waluigi and Wario flew for Star Hill in a helicopter Wario was flying himself, the pilot fired at altitude and stowed in the hold. From the air they saw Mr. L reciting verse in the clinic's street to a courier with a pistol; the road opened a mouth; the helicopter clipped the storehouse roof. Wario dragged Waluigi out under fire and was knocked cold by a steel bar; a jammed pistol spared Waluigi for a speech's length; three copies of Mr. L watched from the stairs. In the street the courier, Paulo, demanded the notebook and 'the coordinates' out of 'this rot-zone', put Waluigi down with a ricochet, took the book from Wario at gunpoint, and walked away reading it. The clinic was never reached.
description:
*The siege ended with a signature and the next thing began with a lurch. This is the record of the leg from my outpost to Star Hill, and it is a record of things lost in order: a pilot to a bulldog clip, a helicopter to a roof, an hour of Wario to a steel bar, three heartbeats of me to a rotor blade, and my working notebook — the one with Luigi in it — to a courier who called me purple boy and walked off reading. We did not reach the clinic. The clinic, as far as either of us could tell, was busy becoming something else. I am filing the street in two halves, because for once the archive's camera was in two places on the same night, and the half I was unconscious for is Wario's and I believe it.*

*What the night settled: Mr. L is not a closed matter. Star Hill has a word for what it has become and the word was given to a courier by somebody with a map. The notebook is gone and the contract is not, which means the sixty-thirty split now exists on a narrative whose notes are in a satchel. The pilot is an open line. I have been told to track the paper trail. For the first time in this partnership I intend to do what Wario says.*

participants.role: Proprietor of the clinic whose front window a courier went through; not seen this night

outcome:
The clinic was not reached. Nobody in this record saw Luigi, and the informant's 'private wing, high security, consciousness fluxing' remains exactly that: an informant's phrase, relayed at volume in a moving aircraft.

Filed as settled: Wario's transport helicopter is a wreck on the storehouse roof beside Dr. Toad's clinic. Waluigi's working notebook — the Luigi notes, the brothers, the poetry Wario once read aloud — is in the possession of a courier who gave his name as Paulo, who read it as he walked away, and who still has whatever his satchel was carrying before the book joined it. A scrap of one page, recovered from a thorn, is the only part of it in the archive. Mr. L was seen by two witnesses in the street and in the stairwell, in a form with lengthened arms and lit eyes and, at one point, in three copies; the road in front of the clinic opened a mouth of flesh and teeth; the storehouse changed its own dimensions while they were inside it.

Filed as open: the fate of the pilot Wario fired and strapped into the rear hold. Whether Luigi is in the building. What 'rot-zone' means, who gave Paulo the word, and what 'coordinates' he expected to find in a notebook of poetry and burns. Who the three green men were watching for, since it was not the pair they let leave.

Also filed, because it is true: Wario gave the notebook up to buy a man he thought might be dying three more heartbeats. Waluigi was unconscious. He is taking Wario's word for it, in writing, which he has never done before.
notableFeatures: 'FIRED HIM. HE'S IN THE BACK.' — the pilot dismissed at altitude by bulldog-clipped notice for saying a hospital is not a landing pad
The notebook on the deck — two fingers on the spine with the door sill in his chest; the book Wario read aloud two weeks ago nearly went out of a helicopter

'I just want to finish my delivery' — Paulo, courier, with a route through Star Hill, a satchel he never put down, and a cheap pistol that jammed once
The mouth in the road — flesh, teeth, an eye on a stalk, opening in the cobbles in front of the clinic; it came out of the ground, not out of him
One hand — the courier thrown through the clinic's front window the way a man tosses a parcel onto a porch
The storehouse roof — the skid on the parapet, the rotor against the chimney stack 'like a bell struck by another bell', the wreck on its side with the red light still going
The steel bar — Wario knocked cold by the frame he had just broken; slapped awake twice; 'I will invoice you for the second one'
'One per cent of my capacity' — a speech about a grimoire and a dead battery, held exactly as long as a cheap pistol took to jam
Three of him — Mr. L on the stairs in three copies, laughing without sound, watching and not following
'We are giving up on the Star-a Clinic' — forty yards from the informant's private wing, the landing getting longer underfoot
'Rot-zone' and 'coordinates' — the courier's two words, given to him by somebody with a map
The notebook as a shield — a round off the fallen rotor blade a hand's width from Waluigi's ear; down for 'three heartbeats of the market'
'Hand it over' / 'Now let's see what you wrote down here, purple boy' — Wario throws the book; Paulo walks away reading
A scrap in a thorn — one torn page the size of a playing card, from the back of the book; the only part of the notebook in the archive
'Hostile takeover. Track the paper trail.' — Wario's reading, and for once Waluigi intends to follow it
'WHO TOOK MY-A NOTEBOOK!' — shouted at a street that did not answer

reputationNotes.waluigi: Held a jammed pistol's attention with nothing but a finger and a speech, then chose a notebook over a surrender and was carried for it; the Enterprise respects a man who will not hand over the asset, even when it was the wrong call.
reputationNotes.wario: A transport helicopter written off on a storehouse roof, a pilot dismissed at altitude and left unaccounted for, and a client-side asset — the notebook — surrendered to an armed courier. The Regency books an unlicensed aircraft down beside a civilian clinic; the Enterprise books the loss and, quietly, the reason for it.
reputationNotes._record: No faction gained standing tonight. Wario's Enterprise lost a machine and a man; the Regency gained another reason to ask what Wario does with helicopters near hospitals. Mr. L, Paulo and the rot-zone belong to nobody the archive can bill yet.

aftermath:
The pair walked out of Star Hill on foot, down the switchback road, in the dark, with the storehouse burning behind them along one parapet and the clinic's windows unlit. Wario's helicopter stays where it fell. Nobody has gone back for the pilot, and this filing says so plainly so that somebody does.

The notebook is gone. The Contract of Accord is not: Wario still holds a signed sixty-thirty split on a narrative whose working notes are in a courier's satchel, which aligns the two signatories more tightly than the signing did — the first paper Wario ever held that pays him more if Waluigi publishes is now also the first that pays nothing until the notes come back. The scrap from the thorn is filed as an exhibit. The custody of the notebook is [[prop:prop_notebook_custody_slip|logged as a loss under duress]], with a named holder, which means the archive can cite it and the holder can be found.

Star Hill is not a clinic any more in any sense this record can defend. The road opened; the building grew; a courier who had never been there before had a word for it. The informant's claim that Luigi is upstairs is unverified and stays on the file as the lead it was before the helicopter left the ground — except that now two witnesses have seen what is standing outside his door.
waluigiAssessment:
**1. We did not reach the clinic and I am not going to dress that up.** The informant said private wing; I have never seen the wing. The file carried a lead called 'the Star Hill lockdown' into this night and it carries the same lead out, with one difference: the lockdown now has teeth in the road and a courier's word for it. Nothing about Luigi is more certain than it was at the outpost. Everything about Star Hill is worse.

**2. Mr. L is on the record from a witness, and the witness was me.** The Regency's file says suppressed. I watched the suppressed man recite in a street and lengthen under fire and stand on a staircase in triplicate, and I watched him go out like a sheet through a window at the end, having followed nobody and harmed nobody but a courier who shot first. He was not there for us. I do not yet know who he was there for, and that question now sits on top of every other question in this arc.

**3. Wario threw my book to a man with a gun, and he was right to, and I would not have.** I have the order of those three clauses exactly where I want it. He bought me three heartbeats I was not awake to spend. The ledger between us was tangled before tonight; tonight it became unpayable in both directions, and I note for the record that neither of us has mentioned the fourteen thousand gold since.

**4. 'Rot-zone' is the most important word in this filing and I was shot at before I could ask about it.** A courier does not coin that. He is issued it, with a route and a map and an instruction not to ask. Somebody at the other end of Paulo's delivery knows what Star Hill has become and has a name for it, and that somebody now also has my notes on the one patient inside it. Wario called it a hostile takeover. I called it worse things, in the street, to the lamps.

**5. The pilot.** He said a hospital was not a landing pad, and he was fired for it, and he was right, and he was in a steel box when the roof came up. I did not go back. That is mine. It is the first line of the next filing whether I want it to be or not.

**Recommendation:** track the paper trail — the delivery, the route, the depot that issues the word 'rot-zone' — before chasing the courier, who is reading my handwriting as he walks and will therefore know what I would do next. Send somebody who is not me to the storehouse roof for the man in the hold. And keep the lead on Luigi open under its old name, because the one thing this night did not do was close it.

imageCaption: The storehouse roof beside Dr. Toad's clinic, minutes after the skid caught the parapet. The transport helicopter on its side with the open door underneath it, the pipe fire taking the parapet, and Wario dragging Waluigi backwards through the gravel by the coat while somebody in the clinic's broken front shoots at the only lit thing on the roof. The red light inside the wreck is still going.

sections.name: I. The Notebook on the Deck
sections.overview:
The sun went down behind the transport helicopter the way it goes down behind anything Wario owns: reluctantly, and with the paint catching the last of it. The cabin smelled of hydraulic fluid and the siege — hot metal, candle smoke still in Waluigi's coat, frost-damp in the lining where the Flash-Freeze had bled through. The side door was latched open because Wario liked to look at what was his from above, and the slipstream came through it in a flat cold sheet.

Waluigi had the notebook open on his knee. Not the revision — the revision was ash and argument now — but the working book, the one Wario had read aloud in a dark room two weeks before and promised not to share. New pages in it. Notes on Luigi: the burns, the two-week rest order, now up, the line about the garden above the fire, a sketch of the clinic's front desk from memory. The pen moved and the deck moved and the pen kept landing on the same word.

*"PRIVATE WING,"* Wario shouted over the rotor, as if briefing a boardroom. *"MY GUY SAYS THEY'VE GOT HIM UPSTAIRS, HIGH SECURITY. UNCONSCIOUS. 'CONSCIOUSNESS FLUXING', WHATEVER THAT COSTS. STABLE, THOUGH. STABLE IS GOOD. STABLE CAN SIGN."*

*"Stable can't sign if he is unconscious."*

*"THAT'S WHAT THE WITNESSES ARE FOR."*

The machine yawed. It was not a bank — a bank is a decision — it was a lurch, the kind a heavy thing makes when the hand on it is thinking about something else. The notebook left Waluigi's knee. It went across the ribbed deck plate on its own cover, spinning, pages fanning, straight for the open door and the black air under it, and Waluigi went after it on his elbows and got two fingers on the spine with the sill biting into his chest and the lights of the valley a long way down past his knuckles.

He came back in on his belly, holding it against his coat with both hands like a man holding a bird.

*WAH! Two weeks ago he read that book out loud without asking, and tonight I nearly went out of a helicopter after it. I am aware of what that says about me. I am filing it anyway, because the alternative is pretending I would have let it go, and the slipstream knows better.*
sections.waluigi_note: The briefing was Wario's informant, secondhand, at volume. 'Private wing', 'high security', 'fluxing' — three phrases I wrote down in a moving aircraft and have never been able to verify, because we did not reach the building they describe. I keep them in the file as what we were told, not as what is true. The distinction cost us a helicopter.

sections.name: II. I Fired Him. He Is in the Back.
sections.overview:
The yaw had an author. Waluigi, upright again and buckling the notebook into the inside pocket where the coin lived, looked forward for the first time since take-off and understood that the cockpit contained one person and that the person was Wario.

*"Where is the pilot."*

*"FIRED HIM."* Wario did not turn round. Both hands were on the stick in the grip he used for slot-machine levers. *"TWENTY MINUTES AGO. HE SAID 'I DON'T THINK WE SHOULD LAND ON A HOSPITAL' AND I SAID 'YOU'RE RIGHT, YOU DON'T THINK,' AND NOW HE'S IN THE BACK."*

The rear hold was a steel box behind a mesh gate. Something in it shifted when the airframe shifted, with the particular sound of a man in a flight suit trying to brace against a bulkhead inside a steel box his own employer had latched on him. He did not shout. He had been working for Wario long enough to know what shouting purchased.

*"You fired him. In the air."*

*"IT'S CHEAPER IN THE AIR. NO SEVERANCE MEETING. I WROTE IT UP."* A square of yellow paper was clipped to the instrument panel with a bulldog clip, flapping, and it was — Waluigi leaned and read it in the green glow of a gauge that was reading something it should not have been reading — [[prop:prop_wario_pilot_termination_notice|a termination notice]], in Wario's hand, with a company stamp, written at altitude. The reason given was *REDUNDANT (OWNER FLYING).* The severance was *TRANSPORT TO DESTINATION (REAR HOLD).*

The helicopter dipped its nose at Star Hill and the whole valley tilted up into the windscreen: the clinic's lamps, the switchback road, a hill that had been quiet two weeks ago. Wario flew the way he drove, which was the way he negotiated — straight at the thing, at full volume, trusting the thing to move.

*"Wario. The clinic is a building. Buildings do not move."*

*"THEN IT CAN WATCH ME COMING."*

*WAH! I have been in a great many vehicles with this man and I have never once been in one that he was licensed to operate. There is a pilot in the rear hold of this helicopter, fired by bulldog clip, and he is the only person aboard who knows what the yellow light means. I know this because I asked, and Wario said 'IT MEANS WE'RE WINNING.'*
sections.waluigi_note: The notice is filed. It is real paper, it has a stamp, and it is the only document in this session that reached its destination intact. I want it on the record that the man in the hold objected to landing on a hospital and was dismissed for it, because by the end of the night he was the only one of us with a defensible position.

sections.name: III. The Green Man in the Street
sections.overview:
They saw him before they saw the roof.

The street in front of Dr. Toad's clinic was lit by two lamps and the clinic's own front windows, and in the middle of it stood a man in black and lime green with his back to the doors, and he was *performing*. Even from four hundred feet it was performance: the stance wide, one arm out, the other hand at his face as if grooming something. The slipstream brought words up in pieces — a rhyme, a bar, a line about a bridge over the king's inferno and a brother who had let go. The voice was Luigi's voice with the fear burned out of it, and it was reciting.

*"That's-a Luigi,"* Wario said, and for once he did not shout it.

*"That is not Luigi."* Waluigi had the notebook out again without deciding to. *"That is the other one. The one the Regency says they suppressed. Wario, look at his hands."*

The green man was talking to someone. A second figure stood at the edge of the lamplight: a wiry man in a courier's jacket with a satchel across his chest and one hand already inside it. The transcript of what passed between them survives because the archive's camera was, for once, in two places on the same night — the second half of this filing is the street, and the first half is the sky — and the two halves meet at a roof.

*"I just want to finish my delivery,"* the courier was saying, in the voice of a man who has said it to a dog, a landlord and a tax office in the same week. *"I've got a route. You are standing on my route."*

The green man turned to him and smiled with too much of his face, and the next verse was for him: brothers, bridges, debts. The courier's hand came out of the satchel holding a pistol.

Up in the cockpit, Wario pulled the stick back to look, and the helicopter — overloaded, mis-trimmed, flown by a man watching a street instead of a horizon — lost the little height it had been pretending to keep.

*WAH! I wrote 'LUIGI?' in the book with a question mark and the question mark went through the page. The Regency filed Mr. L as a closed matter years before this. I was looking down at the closed matter from a helicopter and the closed matter was rhyming.*
sections.waluigi_note: He was reciting. Not shouting, not threatening — reciting, in metre, to a courier who did not want to hear it. I have been told since that this is what the other one does before he does anything else. The archive has never had the other one on the record from a witness. It does now, and the witness was me, and I was upside down for most of it.

sections.name: IV. The Mouth in the Road
sections.overview:
Down in the street, the courier — his name was Paulo, and the record has it because he said it later with a gun in his hand — did what couriers with pistols do when a man in green will not get off the route. He fired.

The round went where he aimed it. The man in green did not go where the round went. He *lengthened*. That is the only word the two witnesses afterwards agreed on: the arms came out of the sleeves further than arms come, and kept coming, and the hands at the end of them had too many knuckles and opened like tools; the eyes went red, not glowing but *lit*, the way a lamp is lit behind a shade; and the mouth that had been smiling at a verse kept widening past the point where a face has room for it. The lime of the shirt stayed lime. That was the worst of it. The clothes stayed Luigi's clothes.

Then the road answered him. The cobbles in front of the clinic split, and what came up through them was not earth — it was flesh, wet and pink, and ringed with teeth, a mouth the width of a cart opening in the street as if the hill had been holding its breath for two weeks and had chosen now. An eye came up beside it on a stalk of the same stuff and looked at the courier with an interest nobody enjoys being the object of.

Paulo fired again, three times, into the long thing's chest. *"Get back! Get the f— back!"*

One hand took him. One. It closed round his ribs and his satchel together, lifted him off the cobbles, and threw him — not hard, almost casually, the way a man tosses a parcel onto a porch — through the front windows of Dr. Toad's clinic in a sheet of breaking glass. The thing in green watched him go, and laughed, and the laugh had Luigi's laugh inside it somewhere, which nobody present will ever forgive.

Overhead, the rotor note changed.

*WAH! I want it filed that the mouth came out of the road and not out of him. He did not make it. He stood beside it like a man standing beside his own car. Whatever is wrong with Star Hill, it was wrong in the ground before he opened his.*
sections.waluigi_note: Two weeks ago this street had a loud triage Toad and a window Ashley preferred to the door. Tonight the road had teeth. I am not filing a theory about what grew under the clinic between the rest order and its expiry. I am filing that something did, and that the one person who might know is unconscious upstairs, if the informant is right, in a wing we did not reach.
sections.imageCaption: The street in front of the clinic as two witnesses described it from the air: the man in black and lime green lengthened past the shape of a man, the cobbles split, and the thing that came up through them — flesh, teeth, and an eye on a stalk — looking at a courier with a pistol. The clothes stayed Luigi's clothes.

sections.name: V. A Roof Is Not a Landing Pad
sections.overview:
The skid caught the parapet of the building beside the clinic — a flat-roofed storehouse, two storeys, tar and gravel — and that was all it took. The helicopter did not fall; it was *tripped*. The tail swung, the main rotor met a chimney stack and came apart with a sound like a bell being struck by another bell, and the fuselage rolled onto the gravel on its side with the open door underneath it and the whole machine screaming.

Waluigi came to with the deck plate against his cheek and the smell of fuel and his own blood in his nose, which is a smell with a copper coin in it. The cabin was on its side. The yellow light had become a red light and was making a noise about it. Above him — it was above him now — the rear hold's mesh gate hung open on one hinge and the hold was dark and he could not see whether the dark had a man in it.

*"WALUIGI."* A hand like a dock clamp closed on his collar. Wario's face was over him, upside down, a cut over one eye bleeding into the moustache, the grin entirely absent, which is how Waluigi knew it was bad. *"UP. NOW. IT'S LEAKING AND THERE'S A GUY WITH A GUN."*

There was. The first shots came off the airframe as Wario dragged him through the crumpled door — sharp flat cracks, the rounds skating off the hull plates with a whine, somebody in the clinic's broken front shooting at the only thing on the roof that was lit. Wario did not run. He pulled, backwards, in a crouch, both hands in Waluigi's coat, Waluigi's heels drawing two lines through the gravel, swearing in a steady undertone that had nothing to do with money.

Behind them a ruptured pipe along the roof's edge let go and caught — a line of blue flame running along the parapet, then yellow, then the tar under it beginning to smoke. The rotor's last blade spun down into the street and rang on the cobbles. The red light inside the wreck kept on about it.

*WAH! Second time this month this man has put me in a helicopter, first time he has put me on a roof with one. He dragged me out by the coat with a hole in his forehead and did not once mention what the machine cost. I wrote that down later with a hand that would not hold still, because it is the kind of thing a filing forgets by morning.*
sections.waluigi_note: I did not see the pilot after the crash. I looked. The hold was open and dark and then there was a man shooting at us and then there was a door. I am filing the omission as mine: a man was aboard that aircraft behind a latched gate because his employer did not want to hear him, and nobody in this record went back for him. That is an open line. It stays open until somebody closes it.

sections.name: VI. The Steel Door and the Steel Bar
sections.overview:
The roof had one way off that was not the edge: a steel door in a brick housing, the kind that opens onto a stairwell, locked from the inside because storehouses are locked from the inside. Wario reached it first and did not try the handle. He put his shoulder into it the way he had put the claw into Waluigi's study door — *once*, to see, and then properly.

The second time the frame came out of the brick with the door still in it and the pair of them went through onto a landing in a shower of mortar. The stairwell below was black and smelled of plaster dust and, under it, faintly, of the pink thing in the road. The building was making a noise. Not the fire; a lower noise, in the walls, like a stomach.

The steel bar came down out of the dark above the lintel — a length of the door's own frame, or a roof beam's strap, or something the shaking had loosened — and it hit Wario across the back of the head with a sound Waluigi has heard on the clay courts when a racket meets a skull, and Wario went down on his face on the landing without a word, which in all the years of the partnership had never happened.

For a moment the only moving thing was dust.

Then Waluigi was on his knees beside him with the notebook digging into his ribs, and he did the one piece of first aid he has ever been trained in, which is the one Wario had performed on him in a dark room two weeks before, in the other direction: he refused to leave. He hit him. Open hand, across the face, twice, the way you hit a man who owes you money.

*"Get up. GET UP. You do not get to lie down. You are-a the one with the contract."*

The second slap got an eye open. The eye focused on him with enormous resentment, which is Wario's version of a pulse. *"...did you just HIT me."*

*"Twice. I will invoice you for the second one."*

The landing shook. Down the stairwell, somewhere on the ground floor, glass was still falling from the window the courier had gone through, and a door was opening, and footsteps that were not in a hurry were coming up.

*WAH! He read my notebook, I slapped him awake. The ledger between us is now so tangled that I think, if you added it up honestly, we would be even, and neither of us will ever do the sum.*
sections.waluigi_note: The bar fell from the frame he had just broken. I note it because the record of this night is otherwise a list of things done to us, and that one we did to ourselves. He has a lump the size of a Star Festival coin on the back of his head, and when I told him so he asked whether it was gold.

sections.name: VII. One Per Cent
sections.overview:
The footsteps belonged to the courier. He came up the last flight with glass in his hair and his jacket torn down one side where the window had taken it, and the pistol came round the newel post before he did, and it stopped with its muzzle a hand's width from Waluigi's face.

*"Who the f— are you!"*

It was not a question. It was the sound a man makes when the night has stopped making sense and he has found something in it that is at least the right shape to shoot. He was shaking, and the shaking did not reach the gun. Paulo, it turned out later. Courier. Route through Star Hill. A delivery in the satchel that he still, through everything, had not put down.

Waluigi, on his knees, with Wario groaning behind him and the notebook over his heart, did what he does when the alternative is being quiet. He stood up into the gun.

*"Waluigi is not a fool,"* he said — and the accent came up with the volume, the way it does. *"You are pointing that at the master of ice. The keeper of the grimoire. The man who froze his own study to save it from a machine with a W on it, and who is standing in a building that is growing while he talks to you. What you are seeing"* — a long finger, raised, between the muzzle and his own eye — *"is one per cent of my capacity. One. You should ask yourself what the other ninety-nine are doing."*

They were doing nothing. There was no MP left in him for a sneeze; the ice wall had taken it all two hours ago. But the finger did not shake, and the courier's eyes went to it, and that was the point of the finger.

Behind the courier, at the turn of the stair, the green man was standing. Then there were two of him. Then — and the record is firm on this, both witnesses, separately — a third, lower down, all three with the long hands and the lit eyes and the same lime shirt, and all three laughing without sound, watching the way an audience watches, the way a man watches people fight over something he has already decided belongs to him.

Paulo pulled the trigger. The pistol clicked. He pulled it again and it clicked again and his face did something terrible.

*"Son of a bitch."* He threw the gun at the nearest green man, turned, and ran back down into the dark he had come up out of.

*WAH! The grimoire is a treatise on atmospheric displacement that I bought at a discount. The capacity was a dead battery and a finger. It worked for the length of time it took a cheap pistol to jam, which is how most of my great moments have worked, and I would like it noted that I did not blink.*
sections.waluigi_note: Three of him. I am writing it plainly because the temptation is to write 'he seemed to multiply' and let the reader decide I was concussed. I was concussed. Wario was not, yet, and Wario counted three. The one in the street two weeks ago was a man with burns. The three on the stairs were something that wears his laugh, and they did not come for us. They watched. I do not know who they were watching for.

sections.name: VIII. We Are Giving Up on the Clinic
sections.overview:
The building moved.

Not shook — moved. The landing lengthened under Waluigi's feet the way the green man's arms had lengthened, the far wall going away from him by a yard, the stair below gaining a step it had not had. Plaster came off the ceiling in sheets. The stomach-noise in the walls climbed toward a voice. Somewhere below, the pink thing in the road was no longer only in the road.

Waluigi took Wario's hand. Not the collar, not the coat — the hand, the big gloved one, and hauled him up off the landing with a strength he does not have and will not have again.

*"We are giving up on the Star-a Clinic. Let's-a go."*

*"THE CONTRACT—"*

*"The contract is in your coat and Luigi is not on this floor and this floor is getting longer. GO."*

They went back the way they had come, through the doorway with no door in it, onto the roof, into the heat. The pipe fire had the whole parapet now, blue at the root and dirty orange above, and the wreck of the helicopter lay in the middle of it on its side with the red light still going, patient, like a thing that would be happy to explain the problem to anyone who would stop and listen. The far end of the roof had a fire ladder. Wario went down it first because Wario goes down everything first, and the ladder, bolted to a building that was changing its mind about its own dimensions, swayed like rigging.

Waluigi stopped at the top long enough to look back at the stairwell. Nothing came out of it. The green men did not follow. The laugh, if it was still happening, was happening somewhere he could not hear.

Then he was down, in the alley, in the dark, with the cobbles under his boots and the stink of the road's mouth thick enough to taste, and Wario was ahead of him pointing at the crash-lit street and saying the only thing Wario ever says in a retreat, which is *THIS WAY, IT'S SHORTER.*

*WAH! I said 'Star-a Clinic.' I heard myself. The accent comes out when I am frightened and I am filing that I was frightened, because the alternative is pretending the floor did not get longer, and the floor got longer.*
sections.waluigi_note: We were forty yards from the building the informant put Luigi in, and we turned round. I want the file to hold that without softening it. I do not know whether a man was upstairs. I know that the stairs were not staying where stairs go, and that I chose the man beside me over the man who might have been above me. If that was wrong, it was wrong in the way I would do again.

sections.name: IX. The Notebook as a Shield
sections.overview:
The street had become a place where things had happened: glass across the cobbles in a fan from the clinic's broken front, the last rotor blade lying in the gutter like a dropped sword, the mouth in the road closed now — or breathing — a seam of pink under a lid of broken stone, and the lamps still on, because lamps do not know.

Paulo was waiting by the wreck's shadow. He had a second pistol, or the same one cleared, and this time he did not put it in Waluigi's face. He put it to his head, from behind, cold through the hair, and spoke low and fast with the shake back in his voice.

*"The book. The one you keep grabbing. Give it here."*

*"It is a working notebook."*

*"I don't care what it is. If it's got the coordinates in it I can get us clear of this rot-zone, all three of us, tonight. That's a good deal. That's the only deal. Hand it over, purple boy."*

*Rot-zone.* He said it like a word he had been told at a depot, by somebody with a map. Waluigi filed the word in the part of his mind that was still filing and felt the barrel move against his scalp as the man breathed.

Wario, ten feet away with the blood dried black into his moustache and the lump on his head coming up under the cap, said the sensible thing, quietly, which is how Waluigi knew the night had changed him too. *"Give it to him."*

Waluigi did not give it to him. He did the stupid thing, and he did it because the book had Luigi in it, and the brothers, and a coin, and two days in a dark room, and a man had already read it once without asking. He brought the notebook up in both hands between the back of his skull and the muzzle — a thin shield, cardboard and wood-pulp — and ran, head down, for the clinic's lit doors, because the clinic was the only building in the street that was still a building.

Paulo fired once.

The round did not take the book. It took the jagged lip of the fallen rotor blade a hand's width from Waluigi's ear — a flat spark and a scream of metal — and the shock of it went through the side of his head like a slammed door. He felt his legs stop being his. He saw the cobbles come up, and the notebook leave his hands and skid away across the stone toward Wario's boots, and then the street folded over him and went out.

*WAH! I have been shot at before. I have not previously been shot at while using my own prose as armour, and I can report that it is a poor material for the purpose and that I would do it again, which is the problem with me in one sentence.*
sections.waluigi_note: He said 'rot-zone' and 'coordinates' in one breath and I was too busy being shot at to ask about either. A courier does not invent a word like that; he is given it, with a route and a reason not to ask. Somebody at the other end of Paulo's delivery knows what Star Hill has become and has a name for it. That is a thread. I was unconscious for the next part, so the next part is Wario's.

sections.name: X. Hand It Over
sections.overview:
What follows is Wario's, given afterwards, without volume, and the archive files it as he gave it.

Waluigi went down flat and did not move. The notebook came to rest against Wario's boot, face down, pages splayed, one corner in the wet from the road. Paulo stood over the body for a count of three with the pistol still out, breathing like a man who has run a stair twice. Then he looked up and the gun came round.

*"Seems like he couldn't take the heat."* He thumbed the slide, checked something, and levelled it at Wario's chest at a distance from which even a cheap pistol does not jam twice. *"Hand it over."*

Wario looked at the notebook. Wario looked at Waluigi, face down on the cobbles with a dark line running from his ear into his collar. He has described the moment since as a calculation, and the archive has let him, because it is kinder than the truth, which is that it was not one.

He picked the book up. He did not open it. He threw it — underarm, the way he throws coins to Toads — and it hit Paulo in the chest and the courier caught it against the satchel with his free hand.

*"Smart,"* Paulo said. He backed away three steps with the gun still up, then turned the notebook over and read the cover in the lamplight, and smiled for the first time all night — a thin, tired, pleased smile, the smile of a man whose delivery has just acquired a second item. *"Now let's see what you wrote down here, purple boy."*

He walked. Not ran. Down the street past the mouth in the road, past the clinic's broken front, reading as he went, turning a page with his thumb, and the lamps took him to the corner and the dark took him after that. The satchel never left his shoulder. Whatever was in it was still in it.

Wario stood in the street with his hands empty and the Contract of Accord in his inside pocket — sixty-thirty on a narrative whose notes had just walked round a corner — and said, to nobody, in a voice the archive has never heard him use about money: *"That was-a mine too."*

*WAH! I was unconscious for this and I believe every word of it, which is a sentence I have never previously written about Wario. He threw my book to a man with a gun to buy me the time I was not awake to use. The ledger between us is not even. It is now unpayable, which is worse.*
sections.waluigi_note: I asked him afterwards whether he considered keeping it. He said yes. I asked for how long. He said 'LONG ENOUGH TO BE OFFENDED THAT YOU ASKED.' That is the most honest accounting of a decision I have ever received from him and I am filing it as such.
sections.imageCaption: The main street, after the shot. The clinic's front window as the courier left it, the fallen rotor blade in the gutter, Wario with his hands empty, Waluigi coming round against the lamp post with a hand to his ear — and Paulo walking into the dark end of the street reading the working notebook as he goes, pistol lowered, satchel still on his shoulder. The book was not hit. It left anyway.

sections.name: XI. Three Heartbeats of the Market
sections.overview:
He came back up through a verse.

It was in his skull before his eyes worked — the green man's metre, the bridge, the brother, and a line that had not been said in the street and that the archive therefore files as the inside of a concussion rather than as testimony: *every page turned is a debt incurred in blood.* Then the cobbles. Then the lamp. Then the shape of Wario crouched over him, upside down again, saying his name without any capitals in it at all.

Waluigi sat up and screamed. *"WAH!"* — the real one, from the floor of the chest, the one that has stopped tennis matches — and the scream did what the slaps had done an hour earlier, which was to remind the night that he was still a party to it.

*"You were out,"* Wario said, *"for three heartbeats of the market. I counted. Prices went up twice."*

Across the street, by the clinic's dark doorway, the green man was standing where the courier had thrown him, one of him only, watching. He raised a long hand — not a wave; a man checking his own fingers — and then the lamplight went through him like a sheet through a window, and he was not there, and the lime of the shirt was the last of him to go. The road did not open again. The building had stopped getting longer. It stood at whatever size it had decided on and kept its windows dark.

Waluigi's hand went to his coat. Inside pocket. Coin — still there. Pen — there. The notebook was not there, and he knew it before his hand did, and he was on his feet before Wario had finished saying *the courier.*

*"Where is it. Where is my— the notes, Wario, the Luigi notes, the— he READ it, he said 'let's see what you wrote', he—"*

*"He took it. I threw it. You were on the ground with your ear open."* Wario had crossed to the alley's mouth, where a thorn bush grew out of a crack in the storehouse wall, and he reached into it with the care of a man taking a coin out of a fountain, and came back with [[prop:prop_notebook_scrap_thorn|a scrap of paper]] the size of a playing card, torn along one edge, lined, with handwriting on it that Waluigi did not need lamplight to recognise. *"He dropped this. Or it tore. It was in the thorn."*

Waluigi took it. The torn edge was his own ruled margin. He read the words on it and put it in the inside pocket with the coin without saying what they were.

*"Hostile takeover,"* Wario said. He had the cap off and was feeling the lump under it, and the voice that came out was the boardroom one, the one that had read the courier's note as a perspective of greed in a dark room and been right. *"That's what this is. Somebody's acquiring. Luigi's in a locked wing, your notes just left in a satchel, and the guy carrying them has a word for this place that he didn't make up. You don't chase the courier. You track the paper trail."*

Waluigi was not listening. He was standing in the middle of Star Hill's main street at night, in the glass, with blood down his neck and a scrap in his pocket and nothing in his hands, and he turned a full circle, and he said it to the lamps and the mouth in the road and the dark windows of the building where a man might or might not have been lying unconscious in a private wing:

*"WHO TOOK MY-A NOTEBOOK!"*

Nobody answered. The thorn kept its other leaves.
sections.waluigi_note: The scrap is filed as an exhibit and I have written down what is on it, which I did not say aloud in the street. It is from the back of the book. It is not about Luigi. I am going to leave it at that in the story and let the paper speak for itself, because that is what paper is for and because I need, for one more filing, to be allowed to be the man who lost it rather than the man who explains it.
